o: We need the count of **distinct** values produced by OR-ing every contiguous subarray of `arr`. With n up to 5·10⁴ there are ~1.25 billion subarrays, so enumerating them all is impossible. The key structural fact: an OR is monotone — extending a subarray can only turn bits on, never off, so values saturate quickly. In Example 3 ([1,2,4]) the subarray ORs are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 — six distinct values from six subarrays. Since `arr[i] < 10⁹ < 2³⁰`, any OR value has at most 30 bits; once a bit is set it stays set, which bounds how many *distinct* ORs a fixed right endpoint can produce.
k: OR is monotone under extension: adding elements only sets more bits, so for a fixed right endpoint the OR grows (weakly) as the left endpoint moves left.
For each index i, the set of ORs of subarrays ending at i has size at most 30: each distinct value must add at least one new bit, and there are only ~30 bits.
We can compute the 'ORs ending at i' set in O(30) time from the previous index's set by OR-ing arr[i] into every element.
Collect all these sets' values into one hash set; its size is the answer.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Subarrays
a.i: Enumerate every subarray by fixing a start index and extending the end while maintaining a running OR incrementally (so each subarray costs O(1), not O(n)). Insert every value into a hash set and return its size. This is simple but O(n²) time — about 1.25·10⁹ operations for n = 5·10⁴, too slow for the given constraints, though it works on small inputs and validates the optimal approach.
s: For each start index i, set cur = 0.
For each end index j >= i, update cur |= arr[j] and add cur to seen.
a.t: O(n²) time — two nested loops with O(1) work per subarray thanks to the running OR.
a.sp: O(D) space for the result set, where D is the number of distinct OR values (up to O(n²) worst case).

a.n: Approach 2: Frontier Sets per Right Endpoint (Optimal)
a.i: Maintain `cur` = the set of OR values of all subarrays ending at the current index. When we move to arr[i], the new set is {arr[i]} ∪ {v | arr[i] for v in cur}. Because OR only turns bits on, each element of this set strictly gains at least one bit relative to some predecessor chain, so |cur| ≤ 30 (values fit in 30 bits). Thus each step does O(30) work, giving roughly O(30n) total. Add every value to a global answer set and return its size.
s: Let ans = empty set, cur = empty set (ORs of subarrays ending at previous index).
For each x in arr: build next = {x} plus {v | x for v in cur}.
Add every element of next to ans.
a.t: O(30 · n) ≈ O(n) expected time — each frontier set holds at most ~30 values since each distinct OR ending at i must introduce a new bit among ≤30 bits.
a.sp: O(30 · n) worst case for the global answer set; the frontier itself uses O(30).

w: In an interview, mention brute force briefly, then lead with the frontier-set approach — it's short, elegant, and provably near-linear. Pitfalls: forgetting that duplicates across different indices collapse via the global set; using arrays/lists instead of sets for the frontier would blow up complexity; watch out for zeros (e.g., [0] → 1, [0,0] → 1). Edge cases: single element, all identical values, all zeros. Follow-ups: count subarrays achieving each distinct OR, or handle updates / streaming input (the same technique works online). A useful sanity check: the answer is at most 30n + something small, so huge outputs signal a bug.
